title: Tesla Reports Q2 Earnings Today as Wall Street Watches Margins and Musk's AI Pivot
excerpt: With record deliveries of 480,000 vehicles but expected margin compression, investors are focused on whether Tesla's AI spending on robotaxis and robots can justify a $25 billion capital plan.
body:
• Tesla reports Q2 2026 earnings after Wednesday's market close, with Wall Street expecting revenue of $26.4 billion (up 17% YoY) and EPS of $0.53 (up 33% YoY).
  • Record Q2 deliveries of 480,126 vehicles — up 25% year-over-year — mark the company's first delivery growth in two years, but analysts worry margins may have slipped.
  • Automotive gross margins excluding regulatory credits, expected around 18%, are the quarter's most-watched metric as the federal EV tax credit's expiration continues to squeeze the industry.
  • Investors want updates on robotaxi expansion (now in seven US cities) and Optimus robot production timelines, which together underpin much of Tesla's valuation.

Tesla is set to deliver its second-quarter 2026 financial results after the market close on Wednesday, with the earnings call scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Eastern. The numbers arrive at a pivotal moment: strong vehicle sales on one hand, mounting questions about profitability and an accelerating AI spending cycle on the other.

The automaker already disclosed that it shipped 480,126 electric vehicles between April and June, its strongest second quarter on record and a 25% increase from the same period last year, according to company filings. Production came in at 451,758 — meaning Tesla sold about 28,000 more cars than it built, drawing down inventory rather than stockpiling it.

The Margin Question

For all the delivery strength, Wall Street's attention is locked on a single line item: automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits. That figure sat around 12.5% in Q1 2026, and analysts expect it to come in around 18% for the second quarter — a number that would still represent a decline from the first quarter's 19.2%, according to Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_S7LlpDErB0

The concern is straightforward. Tesla offered incentives and financing deals to move a record number of cars. If margins compressed, the delivery beat was purchased at the cost of profitability — volume without profit, as Electrek put it in its preview.

Making matters more complicated, Tesla's regulatory credit revenue has been shrinking rapidly. The company booked $439 million in credit sales in Q2 2025, already down more than 50% from the previous year. That decline has accelerated since the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired on September 30, 2025, which knocked EV penetration from 10% of new car sales to under 6%.

"The key investor debate remains unchanged: Can Robotaxi and Optimus progress quickly enough to justify an accelerating AI investment cycle?"

— Andrew Percoco, Morgan Stanley analyst

Revenue and Profit Expectations

Analysts compiled by FactSet project second-quarter revenue of $26.4 billion, up 17% from $22.5 billion a year ago, and net income of $1.8 billion, a 30% year-over-year increase. Non-GAAP earnings per share are expected at $0.53, up from $0.40 in Q2 2025.

The range of estimates, however, is unusually wide. Revenue projections run from $22.3 billion to more than $29 billion, and EPS estimates span $0.27 to $0.74. Deutsche Bank sits at just $0.36 per share. That spread reflects deep disagreement over how much Tesla sacrificed on price to hit its delivery numbers.

Free cash flow is another area of focus. Tesla is not expected to generate positive free cash flow as it ramps spending on AI infrastructure, with analysts projecting roughly $2.9 billion in cash use for the quarter, according to Barron's.

The AI Investment Thesis

Tesla plans to spend approximately $25 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, a dramatic increase from less than $10 billion in 2025. Much of that spending is directed toward robotaxis and the Optimus humanoid robot — the projects that underpin Tesla's premium valuation.

On the robotaxi front, Tesla announced Tuesday that it would expand its ride-hailing service to Tampa and Orlando, after launching in Miami earlier in July. The company now operates in seven US cities, offering unsupervised rides in at least three of them. CEO Elon Musk has said he wants to expand from three states to "probably a dozen states" by year-end, according to MarketWatch.

Progress on Optimus has been slower. Musk pushed back the unveiling of a mass-production version in April, citing concerns that rivals could copy the design. Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Andres Sheppard now expects initial commercial Optimus deliveries in the third quarter of 2027, later than Tesla's earlier forecast of the second half of 2026.

SpaceX Merger Speculation

Adding to the intrigue around the earnings call is growing speculation about a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger. "We think investors are looking at the high possibility of Tesla combining with SpaceX in the near future and what this move could do to the Tesla stock," Deutsche Bank's Yu wrote in a note to clients.

J.P. Morgan has flagged potential regulatory and national-security hurdles tied to Tesla's relationship with China. BNP Paribas analyst James Picariello warned that a combined entity's high cash burn could "further dilute current Tesla shareholders."

What Indian Investors Are Watching

Tesla remains one of the most widely held US stocks among Indian retail investors, many of whom have exposure through fractional-share platforms and US-focused ETFs. The stock has fallen roughly 17% year-to-date, and options traders are pricing in a 7.6% swing in either direction after the report, according to Electrek.

For Indian investors tracking Tesla's trajectory, the earnings call's discussion of capital allocation and margin trends will be more informative than the headline delivery numbers. Tesla's expansion timeline for robotaxis and Optimus will also shape whether the stock's premium valuation — built largely on AI expectations — can hold.

What's Next

Tesla's Q&A session, run through Say Technologies, drew 425 shareholder questions from about 1,710 participants representing 8.6 million shares. The most-upvoted question by raw vote count, with 732 votes, asks about accountability: "Tesla has missed short term guidance on robotaxi 3 earnings reports in a row… what is keeping Tesla back from accomplishing these short term goals?"

The answer to that question — and the margin line on the income statement — will determine whether Tesla's record quarter translates into a stock rebound or another leg down.
